content:
Introduction

1. Using the Simple Past

We use the simple past tense to talk about actions that happened and finished in the past.

Examples:

I watched a movie yesterday.

I visited my friend last week.

She studied English yesterday.

We played cricket on Sunday.

Common time expressions:

Yesterday

Last night

Last week

Last month

Last year

Two days ago

2. Regular Verbs

For many verbs, we add -ed to make the past form.

Present | Past
Play | Played
Watch | Watched
Visit | Visited
Work | Worked
Clean | Cleaned
Study | Studied

Examples:

I played football yesterday.

She watched a movie.

We visited our grandparents.

3. Common Irregular Verbs

Some verbs have different past forms.

Present | Past
Go | Went
Eat | Ate
Drink | Drank
See | Saw
Come | Came
Have | Had
Do | Did
Buy | Bought
Take | Took
Make | Made

Examples:

I went to college yesterday.

She ate breakfast.

He bought a new phone.

We saw a movie.

4. Making Negative Sentences

Use did not (didn't) + base verb.

I didn't go to college.

She didn't watch TV.

He didn't eat breakfast.

We didn't play cricket.

❌ I didn't went.
✅ I didn't go.

5. Asking Questions About the Past

Use Did + subject + base verb...?

Did you go to college?

Did you watch the movie?

Did she call you?

Did they play cricket?

Short answers:

Yes:

Yes, I did.

Yes, she did.

No:

No, I didn't.

No, she didn't.

6. Talking About Yesterday

You can combine different past actions.

Example:

Yesterday, I woke up at 7 AM. I went to college and attended my classes. In the evening, I met my friends. At night, I watched a movie and went to bed at 11 PM.

description: We often talk about our plans, goals, and things we want to do in the future. In this lesson, you will learn how to describe future actions, make predictions, and talk about your intentions using simple English.
content:
Introduction

We often talk about our plans, goals, and things we want to do in the future. In this lesson, you will learn how to describe future actions, make predictions, and talk about your intentions using simple English.

1. Using “Will” for the Future

We use will + base verb to talk about future actions, predictions, or decisions made at the moment of speaking.

Structure:
Subject + will + base verb

Examples:

I will call you tomorrow.

She will help me.

We will visit Delhi next month.

It will rain today.

I will answer the question.

Remember: After will, use the base form of the verb.

❌ I will goes to college.
✅ I will go to college.

2. Using “Going to” for Plans

We use am/is/are + going to + base verb to talk about plans or intentions.

Structure:
Subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb

Examples:

I am going to study tonight.

She is going to buy a new phone.

They are going to play cricket.

We are going to visit our grandparents.

Negative sentences:

I am not going to travel tomorrow.

He isn't going to attend the meeting.

They aren't going to watch the movie.

3. “Will” vs. “Going to”

Both can talk about the future, but they are often used differently.

Use “will” for a decision made at the moment:

The phone is ringing. I will answer it.

Use “going to” for an existing plan:

I am going to study English tonight.

Use “going to” for a prediction based on present evidence:

Look at those dark clouds! It is going to rain.

4. Talking About Future Time

Useful time expressions:

Tomorrow

Tonight

Next week

Next month

Next year

Soon

Later

In the future

Examples:

I will meet you tomorrow.

We are going to travel next week.

She will call you later.

I am going to learn Python this year.

5. Asking Questions About the Future

Use Will + subject + base verb...?

Examples:

Will you come tomorrow?

Will she join us?

Will they attend the event?

Short answers:

Yes, I will.

No, I won't.

Yes, she will.

No, she won't.

To ask about plans, use am/is/are + subject + going to...?

Are you going to study tonight?

Is she going to attend the meeting?

Are they going to travel next week?

Short answers:

Yes, I am.

No, I'm not.

Yes, she is.

No, she isn't.

6. Talking About Your Future Plans

You can combine different future expressions to describe your plans and goals.

Example:

I am going to improve my English this year. I will practise speaking every day. I am going to learn new vocabulary and watch English videos. I hope I will become a confident English speaker in the future.

description: Making plans helps us organize our time and decide what we want to do with others. In this lesson, you will learn how to suggest activities, invite people, discuss availability, and make simple plans in everyday English.
content:
Introduction

Making plans helps us organize our time and decide what we want to do with others. In this lesson, you will learn how to suggest activities, invite people, discuss availability, and make simple plans in everyday English.

1. Talking About Your Plans

Use these expressions to talk about things you intend to do.

I am planning to visit my friend.

I am going to watch a movie tonight.

I plan to study English this evening.

We are planning a trip next month.

I have plans for the weekend.

Examples:

I am planning to visit Delhi next week.

We are planning to organize a college event.

I plan to finish my homework tonight.

2. Making Suggestions

Use these expressions when you want to suggest an activity.

“Let's...” — Suggest doing something together.

Let's watch a movie.

Let's go shopping.

Let's study together.

Let's have lunch.

“Why don't we...?” — A friendly way to suggest something.

Why don't we visit the park?

Why don't we try a new restaurant?

Why don't we practise English together?

“How about...?” — Suggest an idea.

How about going for a walk?

How about watching a movie?

How about meeting tomorrow?

Remember: After how about, use a noun or an -ing form of the verb.

❌ How about go shopping?
✅ How about going shopping?

3. Inviting Someone

Use these expressions to invite people.

Would you like to join us?

Would you like to come to my birthday party?

Do you want to watch a movie?

Are you free this evening?

Would you like to have lunch with me?

Example conversation:

A: Would you like to watch a movie tonight?
B: That sounds great!
A: Let's meet at 7 PM.
B: Sure. See you there!

4. Accepting and Declining Invitations

Accepting an invitation:

Sure!

Of course!

That sounds great!

I'd love to.

Yes, I'd be happy to.

Declining politely:

Sorry, I can't make it.

I'd love to, but I'm busy.

Sorry, I already have plans.

Maybe another time.

Can we meet another day?

Example:

A: Would you like to join us for dinner?
B: I'd love to, but I have some work to finish.

5. Discussing Time and Availability

Use these expressions to decide when to meet.

Are you free tomorrow?

What time works for you?

When shall we meet?

Can we meet at 5 PM?

Does Saturday work for you?

I'm available in the evening.

Example:

A: Are you free on Saturday?
B: Yes, I am.
A: What time works for you?
B: How about 4 PM?
A: Perfect! See you then.

6. Finalizing Plans

Once everyone agrees, confirm the details.

Let's meet at 6 PM.

I'll see you tomorrow.

It's a plan!

See you there.

Don't forget!

I'll let you know.

Example:

We are planning to visit the museum on Sunday. We will meet at 10 AM near the main entrance. After visiting the museum, we are going to have lunch together.

description: Learn how to talk about experiences you have had in your life, college, or daily routine. You will practice using the present perfect tense and the simple past tense to share experiences naturally.
content:
Introduction

Learn how to talk about experiences you have had in your life, college, or daily routine. You will practice using the present perfect tense and the simple past tense to share experiences naturally.

1. Talking About Experiences

We often talk about things we have done, places we have visited, and activities we have tried.

Examples:

I have visited Delhi.

I have tried Japanese food.

She has participated in a college competition.

We have watched that movie.

He has never travelled by airplane.

Structure:

I/You/We/They + have + past participle (V3)

He/She/It + has + past participle (V3)

Base Verb (V1) | Past (V2) | Past Participle (V3)
Visit | Visited | Visited
See | Saw | Seen
Eat | Ate | Eaten
Go | Went | Gone
Try | Tried | Tried
Write | Wrote | Written
Meet | Met | Met
Do | Did | Done

2. Talking About Life Experiences

Use ever when asking whether someone has had an experience at any time in their life.

Examples:

Have you ever visited Mumbai?

Have you ever spoken in front of a large audience?

Have you ever participated in a competition?

Use never when saying that something has not happened at any time.

Examples:

I have never travelled by train.

She has never tried sushi.

I have never given a public speech.

Remember: Use ever mainly in questions and never to describe an experience you have not had.

3. Talking About Recent Experiences

Use just for something that happened very recently.

Examples:

I have just finished my homework.

She has just arrived at college.

We have just completed our project.

Use already when something has happened sooner than expected or before now.

Examples:

I have already submitted my assignment.

He has already eaten lunch.

Use yet mainly in questions and negative sentences.

Examples:

Have you finished your project yet?

I haven't completed my homework yet.

Has she arrived yet?

4. Simple Past vs. Present Perfect

Both tenses describe past events, but they are used differently.

Simple Past: Use it when talking about a completed action at a specific time.

I visited Delhi last year.

She completed her assignment yesterday.

We watched a movie last night.

Present Perfect: Use it when talking about an experience without specifying exactly when it happened.

I have visited Delhi.

She has completed her assignment.

We have watched that movie.

Compare:

❌ I have visited Delhi last year.
✅ I visited Delhi last year.

✅ I have visited Delhi.
✅ I visited Delhi last year.

5. Asking Follow-Up Questions

When someone shares an experience, ask questions to keep the conversation going.

Example Conversation

A: Have you ever participated in a college competition?
B: Yes, I have participated in a coding competition.
A: That sounds interesting! What did you do there?
B: I worked with my team on a software project.
A: Did you enjoy the experience?
B: Yes, I learned a lot from it.

Useful follow-up questions:

What happened next?

How did you feel?

Who went with you?

What did you learn?

Would you like to do it again?

6. Practice Speaking

Try answering these questions aloud in complete sentences:

Have you ever travelled to another city?

Have you ever participated in a competition?

What was the best day of your life?

Have you ever learned something difficult?

What did you do last weekend?

Speaking Tip: Give a short answer first, then add details.

Example:

Question: Have you ever participated in a competition?

Short answer: Yes, I have.

Detailed answer: Yes, I have participated in a college competition. I worked with my teammates on a project, and the experience helped me improve my communication skills.

description: Learn how to explain why something happens, why you make certain decisions, and why you have particular opinions. In this lesson, you will practice using because, because of, so, since, and that's why to communicate more clearly in everyday conversations.
content:
Introduction

Learn how to explain why something happens, why you make certain decisions, and why you have particular opinions. In this lesson, you will practice using because, because of, so, since, and that's why to communicate more clearly in everyday conversations.

1. Giving Reasons with "Because"

We use because to explain the reason for something. It answers the question "Why?"

Structure:

Result + because + reason

Examples:

I stayed at home because I was feeling sick.

She is happy because she passed her examination.

I practice English because I want to improve my communication skills.

We arrived late because the traffic was heavy.

He joined the club because he wanted to learn new skills.

In everyday conversations:

A: Why are you learning English?
B: I am learning English because I want to speak confidently.

A: Why didn't you attend the meeting?
B: I didn't attend because I had some urgent work.

2. Giving Reasons with "Because Of"

Use because of before a noun or noun phrase to explain the reason.

Structure:

Result + because of + noun/noun phrase

Because | Because of
I stayed home because it was raining. | I stayed home because of the rain.
The match was cancelled because the weather was bad. | The match was cancelled because of bad weather.
She was late because her bus broke down. | She was late because of a bus breakdown.

Remember:

Because + subject + verb

Because of + noun or noun phrase

❌ I was late because of I missed the bus.
✅ I was late because I missed the bus.
✅ I was late because of the traffic.

3. Showing Results with "So"

We use so to explain the result of a situation.

Structure:

Reason + so + result

Examples:

I was tired, so I went to bed early.

It was raining, so we cancelled the picnic.

She studied hard, so she passed the examination.

The shop was closed, so we returned home.

I missed the bus, so I took an auto-rickshaw.

Compare:

I stayed home because I was sick.

I was sick, so I stayed home.

Both sentences express the same basic relationship, but they emphasize different parts.

Common mistake:

❌ Because I was tired, so I went to bed.
✅ Because I was tired, I went to bed.
✅ I was tired, so I went to bed.

Avoid using because and so together to connect the same reason and result.

4. Using "That's Why"

Use that's why when you want to explain the result of a reason that has already been mentioned.

Examples:

I didn't sleep well last night. That's why I feel tired today.

She practices every day. That's why her English is improving.

The road was blocked. That's why we arrived late.

I want to become a good speaker. That's why I practice speaking regularly.

Everyday conversation:

A: You speak English very confidently.
B: Thank you! I practice every day. That's why I feel more confident now.

5. Using "Since" to Give Reasons

We can use since to mean because, especially when the reason is already known or is not the main focus.

Examples:

Since it was getting late, we decided to leave.

Since I had an examination the next day, I went to bed early.

Since the classroom was full, we sat outside.

Since you are free today, let's work on our project.

When the reason comes first, use a comma before the main clause.

Example:

Since I was feeling unwell, I stayed at home.

Speaking tip: In everyday conversations, because is usually the easiest and most natural choice when you want to explain a reason directly.

6. Explaining Your Decisions

Giving reasons helps people understand your choices.

Useful sentence patterns:

I decided to ___ because ___.

I prefer ___ because ___.

I chose ___ because ___.

I couldn't ___ because ___.

I would like to ___ because ___.

I think ___ because ___.

Examples:

I decided to learn Python because I am interested in programming.

I prefer studying in the morning because I can concentrate better.

I chose this college because it offers good learning opportunities.

I couldn't attend the event because I had an examination.

I would like to join the competition because it will help me gain experience.

7. Real-Life Speaking Practice

Read the conversation and notice how reasons are used naturally.

A: Why didn't you come to college yesterday?

B: I wasn't feeling well, so I stayed at home.

A: Oh, I see. Are you feeling better now?

B: Yes, much better. I rested properly, and that's why I feel fine today.

A: That's good! Are you coming tomorrow?

B: Yes, because I have an important project meeting.

8. Practice Speaking Aloud

Answer these questions in complete sentences.

Why are you learning English?

Why do you want to improve your communication skills?

Why do students participate in competitions?

Why do you prefer your favourite subject?

Why is teamwork important?

Why should students manage their time?

Why do people travel to different places?

Why is regular practice important?

Challenge: Try to answer each question in two sentences. Give your reason first, then explain the result or benefit.

Example conversation / usage: I left early because I had an appointment.

description: Learn how to communicate confidently while travelling, asking about transport, booking tickets, and finding your way around unfamiliar places. This lesson will help you use practical English in real-life travel situations..
content:
Introduction

Learn how to communicate confidently while travelling, asking about transport, booking tickets, and finding your way around unfamiliar places. This lesson will help you use practical English in real-life travel situations..

1. Talking About Travel Plans

Use these sentence patterns to talk about your travel plans.

Useful Structures:

I am planning to visit ___.

I am travelling to ___.

I would like to visit ___.

I am going to travel by ___.

I have booked a ticket to ___.

Examples:

I am planning to visit Jaipur next month.

I am travelling to Delhi by train.

I would like to visit Goa during my holidays.

I am going to travel by bus.

I have booked a ticket to Mumbai.

Everyday Conversation

A: Where are you planning to go this weekend?
B: I am planning to visit Indore.
A: How will you get there?
B: I will travel by bus.

2. Talking About Different Modes of Transport

Learn how to name different types of transportation and use them in sentences.

Transport | Example Sentence
Bus | I usually travel by bus.
Train | We are going to Bhopal by train.
Airplane | She travelled to Delhi by airplane.
Car | My family travelled by car.
Bicycle | He rides his bicycle to college.
Taxi | We booked a taxi to reach the airport.
Metro | I take the metro to work.
Auto-rickshaw | I took an auto-rickshaw to the station.

Remember:

We usually say by bus, by train, by car, and by airplane.

We say on foot when walking somewhere.

We say ride a bicycle, take a bus, or catch a train.

Examples:

I go to college by bus.

I walk to the market on foot.

She rides a bicycle to school.

We need to catch the 6 p.m. train.

3. Asking for Directions

When travelling, you may need to ask someone how to reach a place.

Useful Questions:

Excuse me, how can I get to the railway station?

Where is the nearest bus stop?

Could you tell me the way to the airport?

Is this the right way to the hotel?

How far is the city centre from here?

Useful Responses:

Go straight ahead.

Turn left at the traffic lights.

Turn right at the next street.

It is next to the bank.

It is opposite the hospital.

It is about ten minutes away.

Example Conversation

A: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to the railway station?
B: Go straight ahead and turn left at the next crossing.
A: Is it far from here?
B: No, it is about a five-minute walk.
A: Thank you for your help!
B: You're welcome!

4. Booking Tickets

You may need to book tickets online or at a ticket counter.

Useful Expressions:

I would like to book a ticket to Delhi.

Are there any seats available?

What time does the train leave?

How much is a one-way ticket?

Can I book a return ticket?

Is there a discount for students?

Could you please confirm my booking?

Example Conversation

Passenger: Good morning. I would like to book a ticket to Mumbai.

Booking Clerk: Certainly. When would you like to travel?

Passenger: Tomorrow morning, please.

Booking Clerk: Would you like a one-way or return ticket?

Passenger: A one-way ticket, please.

Booking Clerk: All right. Here are the available options.

Passenger: Thank you. Could you tell me the departure time?

Booking Clerk: The departure time is printed on your ticket.

5. At the Airport

These expressions are useful when travelling by airplane.

Situation | Useful Expression
Checking in | Where is the check-in counter?
Finding your gate | Could you tell me where Gate 12 is?
Asking about luggage | Where should I collect my luggage?
Asking about boarding | Has boarding started yet?
Asking about delays | Is the flight delayed?
Asking for help | Could you please help me with my boarding pass?

Example Conversation

Passenger: Excuse me, where is Gate 12?

Airport Staff: Go straight ahead and turn right.

Passenger: Thank you. Has boarding started yet?

Airport Staff: Not yet. Please wait near the gate.

Passenger: All right. Thank you for your help.

6. Handling Travel Problems

Sometimes plans change because of delays, cancellations, or lost belongings. Learn how to explain the problem politely.

Useful Expressions:

My train has been delayed.

My flight has been cancelled.

I have lost my luggage.

I think I have taken the wrong bus.

Could you please help me?

Is there another way to reach my destination?

Where can I get more information?

Example Conversation

Traveller: Excuse me, my train has been delayed. Could you tell me the reason?

Staff: There is a technical problem.

Traveller: I see. Could you tell me the expected departure time?

Staff: Please check the station announcement for updates.

Traveller: Thank you for the information.

7. Speaking Practice: Plan a Trip

Imagine you are planning a trip with your friend.

Friend: Where would you like to go for our next trip?

You: I would like to visit Jaipur.

Friend: How will we travel there?

You: We can travel by train because it is convenient.

Friend: Have you booked the tickets?

You: Not yet. I will book them tonight.

Friend: Where will we stay?

You: We can book a hotel near the city centre.

Friend: Great! I am excited about the trip.

8. Practice Speaking Aloud

Answer these questions in complete sentences:

How do you usually travel to college?

Which city would you like to visit and why?

Do you prefer travelling by train, bus, or airplane?

What do you usually pack when travelling?

How would you ask someone for directions?

What would you do if you missed your train?

Have you ever travelled to another city?

What is the most important thing to remember when travelling?

Speaking Challenge: Describe your ideal trip in five sentences. Include your destination, transport, travel companions, activities, and reason for choosing that place.

Introduction

Learn how to communicate confidently in school and college. This lesson covers classroom conversations, assignments, examinations, asking teachers for help, and interacting with classmates.

Learn how to communicate confidently in school and college. This lesson covers classroom conversations, assignments, examinations, asking teachers for help, and interacting with classmates.

1. Talking About Your Classes

Use these expressions to describe your academic routine.

Useful sentence patterns:

I have a class in ___.

My next lecture is about ___.

Our teacher is teaching us ___.

I am studying ___.

My favourite subject is ___ because ___.

Examples:

I have a mathematics lecture at 10 a.m.

My next class is about artificial intelligence.

We are learning Python programming.

My favourite subject is computer science because I enjoy solving problems.

I have three lectures today.

Conversation

A: What do you have in your next lecture?
B: I have a lecture on database management systems.
A: Do you find it interesting?
B: Yes, I do. I enjoy learning how databases work.

2. Talking About Assignments and Projects

Learn how to discuss academic tasks with teachers and classmates.

Useful expressions:

I have to complete my assignment.

When is the submission deadline?

Have you finished your project?

Could you explain this question to me?

I am working on a group project.

We need to divide the work among ourselves.

I have submitted my assignment.

Examples:

I need to complete my assignment by Friday.

Our project deadline is next week.

My team is developing a learning application.

I have finished my part of the project.

We are preparing a presentation for our teacher.

Conversation

A: Have you completed the assignment?
B: Not yet. I am working on the last question.
A: When do we have to submit it?
B: The deadline is tomorrow.
A: Let me know if you need any help.
B: Thank you! That would be helpful.

3. Asking Teachers for Help

When you do not understand something, ask questions politely.

Useful expressions:

Could you please explain this topic again?

I didn't understand the last part.

Could you give us another example?

May I ask a question?

Could you please clarify this concept?

Would you mind explaining this step?

Thank you for explaining it.

Examples:

❌ Explain this again.

✅ Could you please explain this again?

❌ I don't understand anything.

✅ I am having difficulty understanding this topic. Could you explain it once more?

Remember: Polite language helps you communicate respectfully with teachers and classmates.

4. Talking About Examinations

Use these expressions to talk about preparation and results.

Useful expressions:

I am preparing for my examinations.

I have completed most of the syllabus.

I need to revise a few topics.

The examination was easier than I expected.

I found the last question difficult.

I am hoping for a good result.

I need to manage my time better.

Conversation

A: How was your examination?
B: It went quite well, but the last question was difficult.
A: Did you complete the paper on time?
B: Almost. I need to improve my time management.

5. Participating in Classroom Discussions

Learn how to share your thoughts and participate actively.

Useful expressions:

I would like to share my opinion.

I agree with your point.

Could you explain what you mean?

In my opinion, this approach is better.

I have a different perspective.

That is an interesting point.

May I add something?

Example Conversation

Teacher: Why do you think teamwork is important?

Student A: In my opinion, teamwork helps people share ideas.

Student B: I agree. It also helps us solve problems more efficiently.

Student C: I would like to add that teamwork teaches us how to cooperate with others.

6. Talking About College Life

Use these sentences to describe your college experience.

I enjoy participating in college events.

I have made many new friends.

Our college organizes technical competitions.

I am a member of a student club.

I want to improve my communication skills.

College has helped me become more independent.

Speaking Practice

Answer these questions aloud:

What is your favourite subject and why?

How do you prepare for examinations?

What activities do you participate in at college?

How do you manage assignments and deadlines?

What skills would you like to develop during college?

description: Learn how to communicate professionally in workplace situations. This lesson covers introducing yourself to colleagues, discussing tasks, asking for help, attending meetings, and communicating politely with managers and coworkers.
content:
Introduction

Learn how to communicate professionally in workplace situations. This lesson covers introducing yourself to colleagues, discussing tasks, asking for help, attending meetings, and communicating politely with managers and coworkers.

1. Introducing Yourself at Work

When you meet colleagues or join a new organization, introduce yourself politely.

Useful sentence patterns:

Hello, my name is ___.

I work as a ___.

I am responsible for ___.

I recently joined the team.

I look forward to working with you.

It is a pleasure to meet you.

Examples:

Hello, my name is Riya. I recently joined the marketing team.

I work as a software developer.

I am responsible for managing customer requests.

I look forward to working with everyone.

Conversation

A: Hi, I am Rahul from the development team.
B: Hello, I am Aisha. I recently joined the design team.
A: Nice to meet you, Aisha.
B: Nice to meet you too. I look forward to working with you.

2. Talking About Work Responsibilities

Use these expressions to explain your duties and tasks.

Useful expressions:

I am responsible for managing the project.

I handle customer enquiries.

My main task is to prepare reports.

I am working on a new assignment.

I have completed my assigned tasks.

I need some additional time to finish this.

I will update you once it is completed.

Examples:

I am responsible for preparing the weekly report.

My main task is to test the application.

I have completed the first part of the project.

I need another day to finish the presentation.

Remember:
Use responsible for + noun or verb-ing.

Examples:

I am responsible for the report.

I am responsible for preparing the report.

3. Asking for Help Politely

Professional communication should be respectful and clear.

Useful expressions:

Could you help me with this task?

Could you please explain the process?

I need some guidance on this issue.

Would you mind reviewing my work?

Could you spare a few minutes?

I would appreciate your feedback.

Examples:

Instead of: "Check my work."

Say: "Could you please review my work when you have time?"

Instead of: "I don't know what to do."

Say: "I am unsure how to proceed. Could you guide me?"

4. Giving Updates About Your Work

Managers and teammates often need updates about progress.

Useful expressions:

I have completed the first stage.

I am currently working on the next task.

The project is progressing well.

I have encountered a small issue.

I expect to finish it by tomorrow.

I will keep you updated.

The task has been completed successfully.

Conversation

Manager: How is the project progressing?

Employee: I have completed the initial design.

Manager: What are you working on now?

Employee: I am currently developing the main features.

Manager: When do you expect to finish?

Employee: I expect to complete them by Friday.

5. Talking in Workplace Meetings

Meetings require clear, respectful communication.

Useful expressions:

Shall we begin the meeting?

I would like to discuss the project timeline.

Could you explain that point?

I agree with the proposed approach.

I have a suggestion.

Let's discuss the next steps.

Could we schedule another meeting?

To summarize, we have three main tasks.

Example Conversation

Team Leader: Let's discuss our project progress.

Team Member: We have completed the research phase.

Team Leader: What should we do next?

Team Member: I suggest that we start developing the prototype.

Team Leader: That sounds good. Who will handle the design?

Team Member: I can take responsibility for the initial design.

6. Handling Workplace Problems

Problems can happen at work. Explain them calmly and suggest solutions.

Useful expressions:

We have encountered a technical issue.

There seems to be a problem with the system.

I am working on resolving the issue.

Could we discuss an alternative approach?

I apologize for the delay.

Here is my suggestion for solving the problem.

We may need additional time.

Examples:

The software is not working as expected.

We encountered a delay because of a technical issue.

I apologize for the delay. I will complete the task as soon as possible.

We could try a different approach to solve this problem.

7. Professional Email and Message Expressions

Use these phrases when writing workplace messages.

Purpose | Expression
Starting an email | Dear Mr. Sharma,
Making a request | Could you please share the report?
Giving information | I would like to inform you that...
Giving an update | I am writing to provide an update on...
Apologizing | I apologize for the inconvenience.
Thanking someone | Thank you for your assistance.
Ending politely | Best regards,

Example Message

Subject: Project Progress Update

Dear Sir,

I would like to provide an update on our project. We have completed the research phase and are currently working on the prototype.

We expect to complete the initial version by Friday.

Thank you for your guidance.

Best regards,
Aarav

8. Speaking Practice

Answer these questions aloud:

How would you introduce yourself to a new colleague?

How would you ask your manager for help?

How would you explain that a task is delayed?

What would you say during a project meeting?

How would you give an update about your work?

description: Learn how to describe common health problems, make appointments, speak to a doctor, and understand basic healthcare conversations. This lesson will help you communicate clearly and politely when seeking medical assistance.
content:
Introduction

Learn how to describe common health problems, make appointments, speak to a doctor, and understand basic healthcare conversations. This lesson will help you communicate clearly and politely when seeking medical assistance.

1. Describing How You Feel

Use simple sentences to explain how you are feeling.

Useful sentence patterns:

I have a headache.

I have a fever.

I am feeling unwell.

I have a sore throat.

I feel dizzy.

I have been coughing since yesterday.

My stomach hurts.

Examples:

I have had a headache since this morning.

I am feeling weak today.

I have a sore throat and a cough.

My stomach has been hurting since last night.

Remember:

Use I have a headache, not I am having a headache in the usual way of describing the symptom.

Use I feel dizzy to describe the sensation of dizziness.

Use My back hurts to describe pain in your back.

2. Making a Doctor's Appointment

Use these expressions when contacting a clinic or hospital.

Useful expressions:

I would like to book an appointment.

Is the doctor available today?

Do you have any appointments this afternoon?

What time should I arrive?

Could I reschedule my appointment?

I need to cancel my appointment.

Could you confirm the appointment time?

Conversation

Receptionist: Good morning. How can I help you?

Patient: Good morning. I would like to book an appointment with the doctor.

Receptionist: Certainly. Would you prefer a morning or afternoon appointment?

Patient: An afternoon appointment, please.

Receptionist: We have an appointment available at 3 p.m.

Patient: That works for me. Thank you.

3. Speaking to a Doctor

When talking to a doctor, explain your symptoms clearly and mention when they started.

Useful expressions:

I have been feeling unwell for two days.

The pain started yesterday.

I have had a cough since Monday.

The pain gets worse at night.

I feel better after resting.

I have been experiencing frequent headaches.

Could you please explain what I should do next?

Example Conversation

Doctor: What seems to be the problem?

Patient: I have had a headache since yesterday.

Doctor: Have you experienced any other symptoms?

Patient: I have also been feeling tired.

Doctor: When did the symptoms begin?

Patient: They started yesterday morning.

Doctor: Thank you for explaining. Let me assess your condition.

This is an example of communication practice, not medical advice.

4. Understanding Common Health Expressions

Expression | Meaning
Have a fever | Have a body temperature higher than normal
Have a headache | Feel pain in the head
Have a sore throat | Experience pain or irritation in the throat
Feel dizzy | Feel as though you may lose your balance
Feel exhausted | Feel extremely tired
Feel nauseous | Feel as though you might vomit
Have a cough | Cough repeatedly
Feel better | Experience an improvement in how you feel

Examples:

I have a fever and a sore throat.

She feels exhausted after a long day.

He has been coughing since yesterday.

I am feeling better today.

5. Asking Questions at a Pharmacy

You may need to ask a pharmacist questions about medicines or prescriptions.

Useful expressions:

Could you help me understand this prescription?

How should I follow the instructions on this medicine?

Should I take this with food?

Are there any precautions I should know about?

Could you explain the dosage instructions?

Should I consult the doctor before taking this?

Conversation

Customer: Excuse me, could you explain these instructions?

Pharmacist: Of course. Let me explain what the prescription says.

Customer: Should I take the medicine with food?

Pharmacist: Please follow the prescription instructions. If anything is unclear, I can help you understand them.

Customer: Thank you for your help.

Important: Always follow the instructions of a qualified healthcare professional. Do not guess a medicine's dosage.

6. Explaining Absence Because of Illness

Use these sentences when informing your teacher, manager, or colleague that you are unwell.

Examples:

I am feeling unwell and will not be able to attend class today.

I need to take a day off because I am sick.

I have a doctor's appointment this afternoon.

I will complete the pending work once I feel better.

I apologize for the short notice.

Example Message to a Teacher

Good morning, Ma'am.

I am feeling unwell today and will not be able to attend class. I will catch up on the missed work once I feel better.

Thank you for understanding.

7. Rescheduling an Appointment

Sometimes you cannot attend an appointment at the scheduled time.

Useful expressions:

I am unable to attend my appointment today.

Could I reschedule it for tomorrow?

Something urgent has come up.

Is another time available?

I apologize for the inconvenience.

Conversation

Patient: Hello, I have an appointment scheduled for 2 p.m. today.

Receptionist: Yes, how can I help you?

Patient: Something urgent has come up. Could I reschedule it for tomorrow?

Receptionist: Certainly. We have an opening at 11 a.m.

Patient: That would be perfect. Thank you.

8. Speaking Practice

Answer these questions aloud:

How would you describe a headache to a doctor?

How would you book a medical appointment?

What would you say if you could not attend your appointment?

How would you inform your teacher that you are sick?

What questions might you ask a pharmacist about a prescription?

Speaking Challenge: Role-play a conversation between a patient and a receptionist. Make an appointment, explain why you need to see the doctor, and confirm the appointment time.

description: Learn how to communicate confidently when using everyday services, such as shopping, visiting a bank, making enquiries, contacting customer support, and dealing with common problems. This lesson will help you make polite requests and explain situations clearly.
content:
Introduction

Learn how to communicate confidently when using everyday services, such as shopping, visiting a bank, making enquiries, contacting customer support, and dealing with common problems. This lesson will help you make polite requests and explain situations clearly.

1. Asking for Information

Use polite questions when you need information from someone.

Useful expressions:

Could you please give me some information?

I would like to know more about this service.

Could you tell me where the office is?

What are your opening hours?

Is this service available today?

How long will it take?

Is there anything else I need to bring?

Examples:

Could you tell me your opening hours?

I would like to know more about the registration process.

Is the service available on weekends?

How long will it take to process my application?

Conversation

Customer: Good morning. Could you tell me your opening hours?

Staff: We are open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Customer: Are you open on Sundays?

Staff: No, we are closed on Sundays.

Customer: Thank you for the information.

2. Shopping and Making Payments

Use these expressions while shopping or making purchases.

Useful expressions:

How much does this cost?

Do you have this in another size?

Is there any discount available?

Could I see another option?

I would like to return this item.

Can I pay by card?

Could I have the receipt, please?

Examples:

How much does this shirt cost?

Do you have this product in a larger size?

Is there a discount on this item?

Could I pay using UPI?

Could you please give me the receipt?

Conversation

Customer: Excuse me, how much does this bag cost?

Shopkeeper: It costs ₹800.

Customer: Is there any discount available?

Shopkeeper: Yes, we are offering a 10% discount.

Customer: Great! I would like to buy it. Can I pay by UPI?

Shopkeeper: Certainly.

3. At the Bank

These expressions are useful when asking about basic banking services.

Useful expressions:

I would like to open a bank account.

Could you explain the account-opening process?

What documents do I need?

I would like to update my contact details.

Could you help me understand this transaction?

I have a question about my account statement.

How can I report an unauthorised transaction?

Conversation

Customer: Good morning. I would like to open a bank account.

Bank Employee: Certainly. Do you have the required documents?

Customer: Could you please tell me which documents I need?

Bank Employee: I can provide you with the current requirements.

Customer: Thank you. Could you also explain the application process?

4. Using Public Services

Public services include transport offices, post offices, government offices, and other facilities.

Useful expressions:

Where can I submit this form?

Which counter should I go to?

What documents are required?

Could you help me fill out this form?

How long will the process take?

Where can I check my application status?

Is there an online application option?

Examples:

Where can I submit my application?

Which counter handles address changes?

Could you explain how to complete this form?

Is there an online option for this service?

Conversation

Visitor: Excuse me, where can I submit this application?

Staff Member: Please go to Counter 3.

Visitor: Do I need to attach any documents?

Staff Member: Yes. Please check the document requirements listed on the form.

Visitor: Thank you for your help.

5. Contacting Customer Support

Sometimes a product or service does not work as expected. Learn how to explain the problem politely.

Useful expressions:

I am having a problem with my account.

My payment has been deducted, but the transaction failed.

I have not received my order yet.

Could you please check the status?

I would like to register a complaint.

Could you provide a reference number?

When can I expect a resolution?

Conversation

Customer: Hello. I am calling about an order I placed last week.

Support Agent: Certainly. What seems to be the problem?

Customer: I have not received my order yet.

Support Agent: I am sorry about that. Let me check the status.

Customer: Thank you. Could you please tell me when I can expect delivery?

Support Agent: I will provide you with the latest available information.

6. Returning or Exchanging an Item

Sometimes you need to return a product or exchange it for another one.

Useful expressions:

I would like to return this item.

I received the wrong product.

The item is damaged.

Could I exchange it for another size?

What is your return policy?

How long does a refund take?

I have the receipt with me.

Examples:

I received the wrong item. Could you help me exchange it?

The product is damaged, so I would like to return it.

Could you explain your refund policy?

I have the receipt with me.

7. Making Complaints Politely

When something goes wrong, explain the issue clearly without being rude.

Useful sentence patterns:

I am afraid there is a problem with ___.

I would like to bring an issue to your attention.

I understand the situation, but ___.

Could you please look into this matter?

I would appreciate it if you could resolve this issue.

Thank you for looking into the matter.

Examples:

Instead of: "Your service is terrible!"

Say: "I am disappointed with the service and would appreciate your help in resolving the issue."

Instead of: "You sent the wrong thing!"

Say: "I received a different item from the one I ordered. Could you please help me resolve this?"

Remember: Be clear, calm, and respectful when making a complaint.

8. Speaking Practice

Answer these questions aloud:

How would you ask about the price of a product?

How would you ask for help at a bank?

What would you say if you received the wrong order?

How would you ask about a public service?

What would you say if a payment failed?

How would you politely make a complaint?

What questions would you ask before returning a product?

How would you thank someone for helping you?

description: Everyone has opinions about different things, such as education, movies, technology, and daily life. In this lesson, you will learn how to express your opinions clearly, explain your point of view, and give reasons to support your ideas.
content:
Introduction

Everyone has opinions about different things, such as education, movies, technology, and daily life. In this lesson, you will learn how to express your opinions clearly, explain your point of view, and give reasons to support your ideas.

Section 1: What Is an Opinion?

An opinion is what someone thinks or believes about something. Different people can have different opinions about the same topic.

Examples:

I think online learning is useful.

In my opinion, reading books is a good habit.

I believe everyone should learn communication skills.

Personally, I prefer studying in the morning.

Section 2: Useful Phrases for Giving Opinions

Phrase | Example
I think… | I think this book is interesting.
I believe… | I believe practice improves confidence.
In my opinion… | In my opinion, teamwork is important.
From my point of view… | From my point of view, online classes save time.
Personally, I think… | Personally, I think exercise is necessary.
As far as I am concerned… | As far as I am concerned, honesty matters most.
I feel that… | I feel that students need practical knowledge.
The way I see it… | The way I see it, communication builds relationships.

Section 3: Giving Reasons for Your Opinion

A strong opinion becomes clearer when you explain why you think something.

Use these expressions:

Because: I like this course because it is practical.

The main reason is: The main reason is that it saves time.

One reason is that: One reason is that exercise improves health.

This is because: I prefer online notes. This is because they are easy to access.

For example: Technology is helpful. For example, students can attend online classes.

Compare:

❌ I like group projects.

✅ I like group projects because they help students learn teamwork.

Section 4: Expressing Preferences

Use these structures to explain what you like more.

Structure 1: I prefer + noun/verb-ing + to + noun/verb-ing.

I prefer tea to coffee.

I prefer reading to watching television.

I prefer studying in the morning to studying late at night.

Structure 2: I would rather + base verb + than + base verb.

I would rather walk than take a taxi.

I would rather study now than worry later.

Structure 3: I prefer + noun + because + reason.

I prefer practical learning because it helps me understand concepts better.

Section 5: Expressing an Opinion Confidently

You can express your opinion without sounding rude or overly certain.

Situation | Expression
Sharing a personal view | I think this is a good idea.
Showing confidence | I strongly believe that practice is essential.
Giving a personal preference | Personally, I prefer working in a team.
Recognizing another view | I understand that point, but I think differently.
Showing uncertainty | I am not entirely sure, but I think this could work.

Remember: An opinion is not always a fact. Use phrases such as I think, I believe, and in my opinion when expressing personal views.

Section 6: Real-Life Conversation

Situation: Two students discussing online learning

A: What do you think about online learning?

B: In my opinion, online learning is very useful.

A: Why do you think so?

B: I believe it saves time and gives students access to many resources.

A: That's true, but I think classroom learning provides better interaction.

B: I understand your point. Personally, I prefer a combination of both.

description: In everyday conversations, people do not always share the same opinions. Learning to agree and disagree politely helps you communicate confidently without hurting others' feelings. content:
Introduction

In everyday conversations, people do not always share the same opinions. Learning to agree and disagree politely helps you communicate confidently without hurting others' feelings. In this lesson, you will learn expressions for showing agreement, expressing different views, and responding respectfully.

Section 1: Expressing Agreement

Use these expressions when you have the same opinion as someone.

Expression | Example
I agree. | I agree. Exercise is important.
I completely agree. | I completely agree with your suggestion.
You're absolutely right. | You're absolutely right about teamwork.
That's a good point. | That's a good point about saving money.
I feel the same way. | I feel the same way about online learning.
Exactly! | Exactly! We need more practice.
I couldn't agree more. | I couldn't agree more about the value of education.
That's true. | That's true. We should manage our time well.

Tip: “I couldn't agree more” means you strongly agree with someone.

Section 2: Expressing Disagreement Politely

You can disagree without being rude.

Expression | Example
I see your point, but… | I see your point, but I prefer another approach.
I understand what you mean, but… | I understand what you mean, but we need more time.
I respectfully disagree. | I respectfully disagree with that decision.
I'm not sure I agree. | I'm not sure I agree with this plan.
I have a different opinion. | I have a different opinion about this topic.
That's one way to look at it, but… | That's one way to look at it, but there may be another solution.
I agree to some extent, but… | I agree to some extent, but the plan needs improvement.

Avoid: “You're wrong!” or “That's stupid!”

Better: “I understand your point, but I see the situation differently.”

Section 3: Agreeing Partly

Sometimes you agree with only part of what someone says.

Useful expressions:

I agree to some extent.

You have a point, but…

I agree with the idea, although…

That's partly true.

I agree with you on that point.

Examples:

I agree to some extent, but we should also consider the cost.

That's partly true, although the situation is more complicated.

I agree with your idea, but I would change a few details.

Section 4: Asking Whether Someone Agrees

Use these questions to invite others into a conversation.

Do you agree?

What do you think about this?

Would you agree with me?

Don't you think this is useful?

How do you feel about this idea?

What's your opinion on this matter?

Examples:

A: I think students should learn practical skills. Do you agree?

B: Yes, I completely agree.

A: What do you think about group study?

B: I think it is helpful, provided everyone participates.

Section 5: Agreeing and Disagreeing with Reasons

Adding a reason makes your response more meaningful.

Agreeing:

“I agree that students should read regularly because reading improves vocabulary.”

Disagreeing:

“I understand your point, but I think students also need practical experience.”

Partly agreeing:

“I agree that technology makes learning easier, but students should avoid distractions.”

Section 6: Real-Life Conversation

Situation: Two friends discussing mobile phones in college

A: I think students should be allowed to use mobile phones in college.

B: I agree to some extent, but phones can distract students during lectures.

A: That's a good point. However, phones can also help us research information.

B: You're right about that. I think phones should be allowed for educational purposes.

A: I completely agree with you!

description: Comparisons help you explain how people, places, objects, and experiences are similar or different. You use comparisons while shopping, choosing a course, discussing products, and making everyday decisions. In this lesson, you will learn how to compare things accurately and naturally.
content:
Introduction

Comparisons help you explain how people, places, objects, and experiences are similar or different. You use comparisons while shopping, choosing a course, discussing products, and making everyday decisions. In this lesson, you will learn how to compare things accurately and naturally.

Section 1: Comparing Two Things

Use a comparative adjective when comparing two people or things.

Structure: Subject + verb + comparative adjective + than + comparison.

Examples:

My bag is lighter than yours.

This book is more interesting than that one.

English is easier for me than mathematics.

Today's weather is warmer than yesterday's.

This route is shorter than the other route.

Section 2: Short Adjectives

For many short adjectives, add -er.

Adjective | Comparative | Example
Tall | Taller | Ali is taller than Aman.
Small | Smaller | This room is smaller than that one.
Fast | Faster | A train is faster than a bicycle.
Cheap | Cheaper | This pen is cheaper than that one.
Cold | Colder | Today is colder than yesterday.

Spelling rules:

If an adjective ends in -e, add -r: large → larger.

For many consonant-vowel-consonant adjectives, double the final consonant: big → bigger.

If an adjective ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -er: happy → happier.

Section 3: Long Adjectives

For many longer adjectives, use more + adjective.

Adjective | Comparative | Example
Beautiful | More beautiful | This garden is more beautiful than that one.
Expensive | More expensive | This phone is more expensive than mine.
Comfortable | More comfortable | This chair is more comfortable than that chair.
Difficult | More difficult | This question is more difficult than the last one.
Interesting | More interesting | This film is more interesting than the previous film.

❌ This phone is expensiver than mine.

✅ This phone is more expensive than mine.

Section 4: Comparing Three or More Things

Use the superlative form to identify the highest or lowest degree within a group.

Structure: Subject + verb + the + superlative adjective.

Examples:

Mount Everest is the highest mountain above sea level.

This is the cheapest shirt in the shop.

She is the tallest student in the class.

This is the most interesting book I have read.

He is the most experienced person on our team.

Common forms:

Adjective | Comparative | Superlative
Tall | Taller | The tallest
Small | Smaller | The smallest
Fast | Faster | The fastest
Easy | Easier | The easiest
Beautiful | More beautiful | The most beautiful
Difficult | More difficult | The most difficult

Section 5: Irregular Comparisons

Some adjectives change completely.

Adjective | Comparative | Superlative
Good | Better | Best
Bad | Worse | Worst
Far | Farther/Further | Farthest/Furthest
Little (amount) | Less | Least
Much/Many | More | Most

Examples:

This restaurant is better than the one we visited yesterday.

My result is worse than I expected.

She is the best player on the team.

I have less time today than I had yesterday.

This is the most useful feature of the app.

Section 6: Showing Similarity and Equality

Use as + adjective + as to show that two things have the same degree of a quality.

Examples:

My bag is as heavy as yours.

This room is as large as that one.

He is as confident as his brother.

Use not as + adjective + as to show that something has a lower degree of a quality.

Examples:

This road is not as wide as the main road.

My phone is not as expensive as yours.

Today's test was not as difficult as yesterday's test.

Other useful expressions:

Similar to: My opinion is similar to yours.

Different from: This design is different from the previous one.

The same as: My answer is the same as yours.

Section 7: Comparing Options in Real Life

When comparing choices, consider more than one feature.

Example: Choosing a laptop

Laptop A is cheaper than Laptop B.

Laptop B is faster than Laptop A.

Laptop A is not as heavy as Laptop B.

Laptop B has the best performance of the two models being considered, according to the available specifications.

Useful patterns:

Compared with…, …

In contrast to…, …

While A is…, B is…

Both options are…, but…

The main difference is…

Example:

“Compared with the first course, the second course is more practical. While the first course is cheaper, the second course offers more projects.”

Section 8: Real-Life Conversation

Situation: Two students comparing travel options

A: Should we travel by bus or train?

B: I think the train is more comfortable than the bus.

A: That's true, but the bus is cheaper.

B: Yes, and the train is usually faster on this route.

A: Which option is the best for our budget?

B: The bus is the most affordable option, but the train may save us time.

A: Let's compare the ticket prices before deciding.

description: We often need to suggest ideas, recommend solutions, or give advice to friends, classmates, and colleagues. Using the right expressions helps us sound helpful and respectful. In this lesson, you will learn how to make suggestions, give advice, and respond to recommendations in everyday situations.
content:
Introduction

We often need to suggest ideas, recommend solutions, or give advice to friends, classmates, and colleagues. Using the right expressions helps us sound helpful and respectful. In this lesson, you will learn how to make suggestions, give advice, and respond to recommendations in everyday situations.

Section 1: Making Suggestions with “Let's”

Use Let's + base verb to suggest doing something together.

Examples:

Let's study together.

Let's take a short break.

Let's discuss the project.

Let's try another method.

Let's practise speaking English every day.

To make a negative suggestion, use Let's not + base verb.

Examples:

Let's not waste time.

Let's not make a decision too quickly.

Let's not forget the meeting.

Section 2: Using “Why Don't We…?” and “How About…?”

These expressions are useful for suggesting ideas.

Why don't we + base verb?

Why don't we visit the library?

Why don't we practise together?

Why don't we ask the teacher for help?

How about + noun or verb-ing?

How about a cup of tea?

How about watching an English movie?

How about studying for one hour?

What about + noun or verb-ing?

What about going by bus?

What about the cheaper option?

What about meeting after class?

Remember:

✅ How about going for a walk?

❌ How about go for a walk?

Section 3: Giving Advice with “Should” and “Ought To”

Use should + base verb to give advice.

Examples:

You should practise English every day.

You should speak slowly during your presentation.

You should get enough sleep before the exam.

Use shouldn't + base verb to advise against something.

Examples:

You shouldn't skip your meals.

You shouldn't interrupt people.

You shouldn't leave your work until the last minute.

Ought to + base verb has a similar meaning to should.

Examples:

You ought to apologise for the mistake.

You ought to prepare before the interview.

Section 4: Stronger Advice with “Had Better”

Use had better + base verb when you want to emphasize that something is advisable, often because there may be a negative consequence otherwise.

Examples:

You had better leave now, or you may miss the bus.

We had better check the details before submitting the form.

You had better save your work before closing the computer.

Negative form: had better not + base verb.

Example:

You had better not share your password with anyone.

Note: “Had better” can sound stronger than “should.”

Section 5: Making Polite Recommendations

These expressions help you recommend something without sounding forceful.

Expression | Example
I suggest… | I suggest taking regular breaks.
I recommend… | I recommend this book for beginners.
You might want to… | You might want to revise the important topics first.
It would be a good idea to… | It would be a good idea to practise before the interview.
If I were you, I would… | If I were you, I would ask for clarification.
Have you considered…? | Have you considered joining a speaking club?
You could try… | You could try listening to English podcasts.

Grammar patterns:

Suggest + verb-ing: I suggest leaving early.

Recommend + noun: I recommend this course.

Recommend + verb-ing: I recommend practising daily.

You should + base verb: You should practise daily.

You might want to + base verb: You might want to check the timetable.

Section 6: Responding to Suggestions

You can accept or decline suggestions politely.

Accepting:

That's a great idea!

That sounds good.

Sure, let's do that.

Thanks for the suggestion.

I think that could work.

Declining politely:

Thanks, but I have another plan.

That's a good idea, but I'm busy today.

I appreciate the suggestion, but I would prefer another option.

Perhaps we could try that another time.

Section 7: Real-Life Conversation

Situation: A student is nervous about a presentation.

A: I'm really nervous about my presentation tomorrow.

B: You should practise it a few times before going to bed.

A: That's a good idea. What else can I do?

B: You could record yourself and listen to the recording.

A: I haven't tried that before.

B: I recommend it. It can help you notice where you need to improve.

A: Thanks for the advice!

B: You're welcome. You'll feel more confident with practice.

description: Feelings are an important part of everyday communication. Being able to describe your emotions helps you express yourself clearly, explain your reactions, and understand other people better. In this lesson, you will learn useful words and expressions for describing emotions in personal, academic, and social situations.
content:
Introduction

Feelings are an important part of everyday communication. Being able to describe your emotions helps you express yourself clearly, explain your reactions, and understand other people better. In this lesson, you will learn useful words and expressions for describing emotions in personal, academic, and social situations.

Section 1: Common Feelings and Emotions

Emotion | Meaning | Example
Happy | Feeling pleased | I feel happy about my result.
Sad | Feeling unhappy | She felt sad after saying goodbye.
Angry | Feeling strong displeasure | He was angry about the unfair decision.
Excited | Feeling enthusiastic about something | I'm excited about the college event.
Nervous | Feeling worried or anxious | I feel nervous before interviews.
Relaxed | Feeling calm and comfortable | I feel relaxed after a walk.
Disappointed | Feeling unhappy because something was not as expected | I was disappointed with my score.
Proud | Feeling pleased about an achievement | I'm proud of my progress.
Embarrassed | Feeling uncomfortable or self-conscious | She felt embarrassed after forgetting his name.
Confused | Unable to understand something clearly | I'm confused about these instructions.

Section 2: How to Describe Your Feelings

Use these common structures.

Structure 1: I feel + adjective.

I feel confident.

I feel nervous.

I feel disappointed.

Structure 2: I am + adjective.

I am excited about the trip.

I am worried about the exam.

I am grateful for your help.

Structure 3: I feel + adjective + because…

I feel happy because I passed the test.

I feel nervous because I have an interview tomorrow.

I feel disappointed because the event was cancelled.

Structure 4: It makes me feel + adjective.

Listening to music makes me feel relaxed.

Positive feedback makes me feel confident.

Being ignored makes me feel upset.

Section 3: Expressing Different Levels of Emotion

You can use adverbs to explain how strongly you feel.

Expression | Example
A little | I'm a little nervous.
Slightly | I'm slightly worried about the result.
Quite | I'm quite excited about the trip.
Very | I'm very happy with my progress.
Really | I'm really grateful for your support.
Extremely | I'm extremely proud of our team's achievement.
Absolutely | I'm absolutely delighted with the news.

Note: Some adjectives commonly pair with particular adverbs. For example, “absolutely delighted” sounds natural, while “very delighted” is less common in many contexts.

Section 4: Positive Emotions

Use these words to communicate positive feelings.

Word | Meaning | Example
Grateful | Feeling thankful | I'm grateful for your support.
Confident | Believing in your own ability | I feel confident about my presentation.
Relieved | Feeling better after worry or stress has ended | I'm relieved that the exam is over.
Motivated | Feeling eager to take action | I feel motivated to improve my English.
Delighted | Very pleased | I'm delighted to hear the news.
Hopeful | Expecting something good may happen | I'm hopeful about the future.

Section 5: Negative and Difficult Emotions

Use these words to explain difficult feelings.

Word | Meaning | Example
Anxious | Worried or uneasy about something | I'm anxious about the interview.
Frustrated | Annoyed because something is difficult or not working | I'm frustrated because the app isn't working.
Overwhelmed | Feeling that there is too much to handle | I feel overwhelmed by all the assignments.
Lonely | Feeling alone or lacking companionship | He felt lonely in the new city.
Guilty | Feeling that you have done something wrong | I felt guilty for missing the meeting.
Insecure | Lacking confidence or feeling uncertain about yourself | She feels insecure when speaking in public.

Section 6: Explaining Feelings Without Blaming Others

Good communication means describing your feelings respectfully.

Instead of saying:

❌ “You always make me angry!”

Try saying:

✅ “I feel upset when my concerns are not heard.”

Instead of:

❌ “You don't care about me!”

Try saying:

✅ “I feel ignored when I don't receive a response.”

Instead of:

❌ “This is all your fault!”

Try saying:

✅ “I'm frustrated with the situation. Can we discuss how to solve it?”

Useful structure:

“I feel ___ when ___ because ___.”

Examples:

I feel worried when plans change suddenly because I need time to prepare.

I feel disappointed when a promise is broken because trust is important to me.

I feel appreciated when people acknowledge my efforts.

This approach helps you explain your feelings without immediately blaming another person.

Section 7: Talking About Other People's Feelings

You can describe how another person may feel, while remembering that you cannot always know their emotions for certain.

Examples:

She seems nervous about the interview.

He looks excited about the competition.

They might feel disappointed about the result.

You seem worried. Would you like to talk about it?

I can understand why you feel frustrated.

Useful expressions:

You seem…

You look…

I imagine you might feel…

I can understand why…

Would you like to talk about it?

Section 8: Responding to Someone's Feelings

When someone shares an emotion, respond with empathy.

Situation | Helpful Response
Someone feels nervous | It's understandable to feel nervous.
Someone feels disappointed | I'm sorry things didn't go as expected.
Someone shares good news | That's wonderful! I'm happy for you.
Someone feels overwhelmed | Would it help to break the work into smaller tasks?
Someone is grateful | You're welcome. I'm glad I could help.
Someone feels frustrated | That sounds difficult. Let's see what we can do.

Section 9: Real-Life Conversation

Situation: Two friends discussing an upcoming interview

A: How are you feeling about your interview tomorrow?

B: Honestly, I'm quite nervous.

A: That's understandable. Interviews can be stressful.

B: I'm worried that I might forget my answers.

A: You could practise a few common questions tonight.

B: That's a good idea. I think I'll feel more confident after practising.

A: Exactly. And remember, you don't have to give perfect answers. Just be clear and genuine.

B: Thanks. I already feel a little more relaxed.
